video.title: Lists: A tool for your marks
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Forty marks, and the head teacher wants the class average, the top mark and how many failed, by noon. With forty separate variables I’d still be typing. A list holds all forty in one name.
Today: lists, a tool for your marks.

scenes.on_screen_text: A list: many values, one name
scenes.narration: A list keeps many values, in order, under one name. Write them in square brackets, with commas between. Each value has a position, and positions count from zero. So marks at zero is the first mark.
Python already knows the jobs teachers do with marks. len counts them. sum adds them up. max and min find the highest and the lowest. And sum divided by len is the average.

To do something with each mark, loop over the list. for m in marks gives you each mark in turn. Here, the loop counts the pupils below ten, the pass mark. Counting is a running total that adds one each time.

scenes.on_screen_text: Add marks, or read a file
scenes.narration: You can add to a list as marks come in, with append. Or keep the marks in a small file, one pupil per line, and let Python read it. A spreadsheet can save that file as CSV. Then the same program works for every class.
Quick check! The list is fourteen, nine, seventeen. What does marks at one give?
Nine. Position zero is the first mark, so position one is the second. And there’s no position three in a list of three: asking for it stops the program with an IndexError.

scenes.on_screen_text: What lists can do for you
scenes.narration: With lists, a short program does real work. The class average and the top mark. How many pupils are below the pass mark. Marks sorted from lowest to highest with sorted. All on your phone, with no internet.
A word on privacy. Practise with made-up marks, or first names only. A program on your phone keeps the data on your phone. Don’t paste a class list with full names into a website you don’t trust.
In the app, open Sorting race. Python’s sorted does this work for you, but the race shows what happens inside. Race eight bars, then thirty-two, and watch the counts grow.
Your turn. The marks are ten, twelve and fourteen. What does sum of marks divided by len of marks print?

scenes.on_screen_text: One name · from 0 · len, sum, max · made-up data
scenes.narration: Twelve point zero. Remember: a list keeps many values under one name, and positions count from zero. len, sum, max and min do the common jobs. A loop over a list counts and totals. And practise with made-up data.
Try it in class tomorrow: a class survey. Pupils vote for their favourite fruit, and you type the votes into a list. Let Python count each fruit with a loop, and show the class the result.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — positions count from 0, so position 1 is the second mark: 9.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — position 0 is 14, so position 1 is the second mark: 9.

checkpoints.prompt: marks = [10, 12, 14]. What does sum(marks) / len(marks) print?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 36 divided by 3 is 12, and / gives 12.0.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — sum is 36 and len is 3: 36 / 3 = 12.0.
